practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Richard Nixon, 3 November 1969.
‘The defence of freedom is everybody’s business — not just America’s business. Under our new policy, we shall provide assistance to those Asian nations capable of and willing to participate in their own defence. The South Vietnamese have continued to gain in strength. As a result they have been able to take over combat responsibilities from our American troops.’

Source A suggests that Nixon presented Vietnamisation as a policy that shared the burden rather than an American retreat. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He says the defence of freedom is ‘everybody’s business — not just America’s business’.
• Assistance will go to Asian nations ‘capable of and willing to participate in their own defence’.
• He claims the South Vietnamese have grown strong enough to take over combat duties.
Contextual knowledge: Nixon announced Vietnamisation on 3 November 1969; US troop numbers fell from a peak of 540,000 to under 50,000 by mid-1972 while the ARVN grew to over a million men.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Nixon’s decision to invade Cambodia in April 1970 led to the largest student strike in US history.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise dates and details (Cambodia announcement, Kent State, Jackson State, the campus strike, Congress’s response).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology.

Indicative content:
• March 1969: Nixon began secret B-52 bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu), concealed from Congress.
• 30 April 1970: Nixon announced the Cambodia incursion in a televised address.
• 1–4 May 1970: campus protests erupted across the United States.
• 4 May 1970: Ohio National Guardsmen shot four unarmed students dead at Kent State University.
• 5–15 May 1970: nationwide student strike spread to around 900 campuses; over four million students walked out.
• 14–15 May 1970: police killed two students at Jackson State College in Mississippi.
• June 1970: the Senate voted to repeal the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and passed the Cooper-Church Amendment to limit operations in Cambodia; the repeal took effect in January 1971.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1972 New York Times news analysis of Nixon’s February 1972 visit to Beijing.
‘The visit changes the shape of the Cold War. Hanoi can no longer assume Chinese support is unconditional. Moscow must now compete for American friendship rather than count on it. The Vietnam War, while continuing, is no longer the central event of American foreign policy.’

Source C: An extract from a Vietnamese diplomat’s memoir, published in Hanoi in the 1990s, recalling Politburo discussions in spring 1972.
‘Comrade Mao’s reception of the American president disturbed us. We were told the Chinese would maintain their aid — but we were also told to prepare for the possibility that Beijing’s priorities had shifted. We knew the war must now be ended on terms we could secure quickly.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of Nixon’s opening to China on the Vietnam War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: argues the Beijing visit reshaped Cold War alignments and pressured Hanoi. Provenance: a New York Times news analysis written immediately after the visit, for a US public audience — useful for showing how the move was understood at the time, but reflects American framing. Own knowledge: Kissinger had visited Beijing secretly in July 1971; the Sino-Soviet split made the opening possible; Linebacker II in December 1972 followed within ten months.
Source C — Content: shows Hanoi acknowledging the disturbance the visit caused. Provenance: a Politburo-level memoir published in the 1990s, written with hindsight and likely smoothed for publication — useful as the Vietnamese view, but not contemporary documentary evidence. Own knowledge: the Paris Peace Accords were signed January 1973; Hanoi did indeed feel the urgency of a settlement.
Judgement: B is highly useful for immediate US understanding; C is highly useful for the Vietnamese response, with the caveat that hindsight may shape its emphasis. Together they show the opening worked diplomatically even as the war continued.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a televised report on the Kent State shootings, broadcast on NBC News, 4 May 1970.
‘Today four students at Kent State University in Ohio were shot dead by Ohio National Guardsmen during a protest against the war in Cambodia. Nine others were wounded. Witnesses describe the soldiers turning and firing into a crowd that included students walking to class. The university is closed indefinitely.’

Source D suggests that the Cambodian incursion turned protest at home into violence. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Four students were shot dead by National Guardsmen during a protest against the war in Cambodia.
• Nine others were wounded, and witnesses describe soldiers firing into a crowd that included students walking to class.
• The university closed indefinitely.
Contextual knowledge: Nixon had announced the incursion on 30 April 1970; over four million students walked out afterwards, and two more students were killed at Jackson State on 14–15 May.

practice_questions.text:
‘The decision to invade Cambodia was the most damaging moment of Nixon’s Vietnam policy.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The incursion, announced on 30 April 1970, reignited a campus movement that Vietnamisation had been quietening.
• Four students were killed at Kent State on 4 May and two at Jackson State on 14–15 May.
• Over four million students walked out, the largest student strike in American history.
• Congress moved against presidential war power: the Senate voted to repeal the Tonkin Resolution and passed the Cooper-Church Amendment.
Disagree:
• Watergate did more lasting harm: it forced Nixon’s resignation in August 1974 and destroyed the political capacity to enforce the 1973 Accords.
• The Christmas bombings of December 1972 caused comparable international outrage.
• Vietnamisation had already conceded that the United States would not win the ground war.
• The secret bombing of Cambodia from March 1969 had begun the widening before 1970.
Judgement: Cambodia was the most damaging moment for the home front; Watergate was more damaging for the outcome of the war.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the diplomatic and military steps Nixon took between 1969 and 1972 to extract the United States from Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (Vietnamisation announcement, secret bombing of Cambodia, Kissinger’s 1971 Beijing visit, Easter Offensive, Linebacker II).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• March 1969: Nixon authorised secret B-52 bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu).
• 3 November 1969: Nixon announced the Vietnamisation policy on television.
• April 1970: Cambodian incursion by US ground troops.
• July 1971: Kissinger visited Beijing secretly.
• February 1972: Nixon visited China; opened relations with Mao.
• Spring 1972: North Vietnamese Easter Offensive.
• April–October 1972: Linebacker I bombing of North Vietnam.
• December 1972: Linebacker II ‘Christmas Bombings’ of Hanoi and Haiphong forced Hanoi back to the negotiating table.
• Through this period US troop numbers fell from 540,000 to under 50,000.
